QuickSight continues as Amazon Quick Sight, a feature within Quick.” Same shape as the SageMaker case — the BI tool is now one feature of a larger AI product (alongside Quick Flows, Quick Automate, Quick Index, Quick Research). Independently corroborated by the Lake Formation docs, whose enforcement list now reads “Amazon Athena, Amazon Quick, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue”. name: Amazon Quick Sight
oneLiner: Serverless BI dashboards and visual analytics over AWS data.
whatItIs: QuickSight is AWS's serverless business-intelligence service — the dashboard-and-charts layer at the very end of the pipeline. It connects to Redshift, Athena, RDS, S3 and other sources, lets analysts build interactive dashboards, and serves them to business users in the browser. Its in-memory engine, SPICE, caches datasets for fast queries without hammering the warehouse. It's fully managed with no servers to run, per-session pricing options for occasional viewers, and increasingly embeds natural-language Q&A (Amazon Q). QuickSight is where curated data becomes the charts decision-makers actually look at. On the naming: AWS has folded this into a larger AI service. Amazon Quick is now the umbrella product — automation, research, app building and analytics — and the BI tool continues inside it as Amazon Quick Sight. Existing QuickSight APIs, SDKs and integrations are unchanged, so code and docs URLs still say quicksight.

inPractice.narrative: Data has been cleaned and modelled in Redshift. An analyst connects QuickSight to it, ingests key tables into SPICE for speed, and builds a sales dashboard with filters and drill-downs. Business users open it in the browser to explore the numbers themselves — no SQL, no warehouse access. QuickSight is the serving/presentation layer: it turns the warehouse's tables into the visuals people make decisions from.

coreConcepts.detail: An in-memory, columnar cache that holds datasets for fast, concurrent dashboard queries without re-hitting the source each time — the key to responsiveness and cost control.
Connects to Redshift, Athena, RDS/Aurora, S3, and many databases/SaaS; you can query live (direct) or ingest into SPICE.
Datasets prepare/model data; analyses are the authoring canvas; dashboards are the published, shareable read-only views.
No servers to manage; authors are billed by user, and readers can be billed per session (pay-per-session) — cost-effective for occasional viewers.
Restrict which rows each user sees so one dashboard safely serves many teams/customers.
Natural-language questions and generative summaries let users ask for insights in plain English over their data.

whenToUse: Dashboards and visual analytics over AWS-hosted data.
Serving interactive reports to business users without warehouse access.
Fast dashboards via SPICE caching to offload the warehouse.
Occasional viewers where per-session pricing beats per-seat.
Embedding analytics into apps or portals.
whenNotToUse: Heavy data transformation/modelling — do that upstream in the warehouse/ETL, not the BI tool.
Pixel-perfect operational/print reporting beyond dashboarding needs.
Deep semantic-modelling governance where a dedicated modelling layer (e.g. LookML) is required.
Data outside AWS with no easy connector as the primary source.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per author + per reader (pay-per-session or per-user) + SPICE capacity.

pricingShape: QuickSight bills by users and SPICE capacity: authors pay a per-user subscription, while readers can be billed either per-user or pay-per-session (capped monthly) — the session model is what makes it cheap to give thousands of occasional viewers access. SPICE storage beyond the included allotment adds cost. There's no server to run. The main levers are choosing per-session vs per-user reader pricing by how often people view, and using SPICE to keep dashboards fast without driving up warehouse query cost.
gotchas: SPICE has capacity limits and needs refreshing — stale or oversized SPICE datasets cause wrong or failing dashboards.
Do transformation upstream; modelling heavily inside QuickSight gets unwieldy fast.
Direct-query (non-SPICE) dashboards push load and cost onto the warehouse on every interaction.
Reader pricing model choice (session vs user) materially changes the bill — pick by actual viewing frequency.
Row-level security must be set up correctly or a shared dashboard leaks data across teams.
